readerTitle: One bottle, four ways to sell it: pick one
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (천연 세정 농축액 브랜드, 청소 대행업체, 지역 철물점 체인) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 작은 사업의 첫 유통은 여러 채널에 나눠 거는 것이 아니라, 고객이 이미 제품을 믿게 되는 한 곳을 골라 그 채널이 반복 가능해질 때까지 파고드는 것이다.
misconception: 채널이 많을수록 더 많이 팔린다. 큰 소매 체인이 들어오라고 하면 무조건 기회다.

sources.text: 마케팅·유통의 표준 개념 (채널 적합성, 중간 유통 마진, 고객 관계 소유)
모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 병당 제조원가 $4, 소비자가 $16, 청소업체 공급가 $10 → Maya 몫 $10 − $4 = $6, 청소업체 몫 $16 − $10 = $6. 계산을 다시 확인하세요.
철물점 체인 제안: 공급가 $8 → Maya 몫 $8 − $4 = $4. 선주문 2,000병 × 제조원가 $4 = $8,000으로 보유 자금 $15,000의 절반 이상. 계산을 다시 확인하세요.
리필 코드 수수료 $2: 직접 판매 $16 − $4 − $2 = $10이 Maya 몫. 배송비 등은 단순화를 위해 제외했습니다.

cards.title: One bottle, four ways to sell it: pick one
body: Maya makes a plant-based cleaning concentrate. One bottle, mixed with water, cleans a home for about two months. It works as well as the big brands.
She has $15,000, a garage stacked with bottles, and four ways she could sell them. She can afford to do **one** of them well. You're making her calls.

image.label: A garage of cleaning bottles with four paths leading out
image.brief: 차고 안에 라벨 없는 세정제 병이 쌓여 있고, 문밖으로 갈림길 네 개(가게 진열대, 노트북 화면, 청소 대행 밴, 창고 트럭)가 뻗어 나감. 따뜻한 일러스트 톤. 실제 브랜드 로고와 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Where does the first bottle get sold?
body: Two problems: people doubt that plant-based cleaners really work, and few know how to dilute a concentrate. Maya's bottle needs someone to *show* it working.

options.text: Get onto local grocery and hardware shelves
options.feedback: The bottle sits beside famous brands with no one to explain it. Shoppers pass it by, and unsold stock comes back.

options.text: Open an online store and run social ads
options.feedback: It can work, but strangers need many ads before they trust an unknown cleaner. Each customer costs more than Maya can afford for long.

options.text: Sell to local house-cleaning companies who use it in clients' homes
options.feedback: Cleaners prove it works every visit, in front of the people who'd buy it. The channel fits the product's biggest problem.

cards.title: Say you chose the cleaners. Now set their price.
body: Clients ask their cleaners where to buy it. Each bottle costs Maya $4 to make and sells to households for $16. What should cleaners pay?

options.text: $14, so Maya keeps most of the money
options.feedback: Maya earns $10 a bottle, but cleaners earn $2 for the hassle of reselling. Most stop bothering.
Maya gives up margin, but cleaners now have a real reason to recommend and stock it. Twelve companies sign on in two months.

options.text: Skip the cleaners and sell to their clients directly at $16
options.feedback: Maya keeps $12 a bottle, until cleaners notice. They stop using the product they're being cut out of.

cards.title: Say you shared the margin. Who knows the buyer?
body: Sales grow, but every reorder goes through a cleaner. Maya has no names, no emails, and no idea which homes buy most.

options.text: Leave it. The cleaners own those relationships
options.feedback: Simple and friendly. But if a big cleaner switches brands, Maya loses customers she never knew she had.

options.text: Add a refill code on each bottle. Reorders go to Maya's site, and the cleaner earns $2
options.feedback: Maya learns who buys, and cleaners still get paid. After the commission she keeps $10 on each refill.

options.text: Add a code with a discount that beats the cleaners' price
options.feedback: Maya gets the data, but she's undercutting her own channel. Cleaners feel betrayed and the recommendations dry up.

cards.title: Say you added the code. A chain calls.
body: A regional hardware chain offers shelves in 40 stores. It wants to pay $8 a bottle and needs 2,000 bottles upfront. That's $8,000 of Maya's cash tied up in stock.

options.text: Say yes. Forty stores is huge
options.feedback: Maya keeps $4 a bottle and stretches her cash. And the shelf problem from Decision 1 hasn't gone away.

options.text: Say not yet. Grow the cleaner channel, and come back with reorder proof
options.feedback: Maya keeps her cash and focus where sales already repeat. Later, refill data gives her a stronger case for the chain.
Cheaper to learn from, but it still splits Maya's attention. A good move once the first channel runs without her.

cards.softwareNote: Software founders face the same call: app marketplaces, resellers, direct sales. Getting one to bring in users steadily usually beats a thin presence in all of them.

cards.title: One channel, done well, opened the next.
body: A year on, Maya sells through 30 cleaning companies. Refill codes show which neighborhoods reorder most and how often.
When she goes back to the hardware chain, she brings that data. Now it's a pitch based on proof, not hope.
The lesson: an early business rarely fails for picking the wrong channel. It fails by spreading thin money and time across **too many channels** before any one works.

image.label: One strong path growing into a second path
image.brief: 굵은 길 하나(청소 대행 밴 → 집들)가 끝에서 두 번째 길(가게 진열대)로 자연스럽게 이어지는 그림. 길 위에 작은 리필 병 아이콘들. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: One channel is a start, not a forever plan.
body: Depending on one channel is a risk. If a few big partners drive most sales, they can squeeze your price or walk away.
Focus works when the channel is still growing and you're learning from it. Once growth stalls, or one partner holds too much power, it's time to test a second channel.
And "one channel" doesn't mean ignoring others forever. It means saying *not yet* on purpose.

cards.title: Win one channel before you add another.
body: Each of Maya's calls maps to an idea from this unit:
list: **Decision 1:** Channel fit. Sell where your product's biggest problem gets solved.
**Decision 2:** Middlemen and margins. Partners need a real cut to push you.
**Decision 3:** Owning the customer. Know your buyers without cutting out partners.
**Decision 4:** Choosing channels. Say *not yet* until one channel repeats.
cards.callout: **Try it today:** list every channel you sell through. Circle the one bringing in repeat customers. What would doubling down on it look like?
